web_evidence.title: 'Black House' by Stephen King and Peter Straub
web_evidence.note: Authorized, permission-granted opening excerpt sustains an external aerial survey, moves the reader-inclusive narrator through French Landing, and presents Bobby Dulac and Tom Lund externally.

web_evidence.title: BLACK HOUSE
web_evidence.note: The professional review explicitly describes the device as an unusual “third-person plural narration” that continues throughout the book.

web_evidence.title: 'Black House' a bright spot in horror
web_evidence.note: The contemporary review characterizes the book’s controlling voice as plural and omniscient, consistent with a nonparticipating third-person narrator despite its use of “we.”

web_evidence.title: King, Stephen (1947–)
web_evidence.note: Literary analysis explains that the narration equates reader and narrator in a first-person-plural rhetorical device and quotes the voice observing a murder scene; under the task’s participation criterion, this is an external observer rather than a character narrator.

web_evidence.title: King and Straub let their horrors run wild
web_evidence.note: The review reports shifting point of view among a gallery of heroes and villains, corroborating omniscient external focalization rather than autonomous first-person character sections.

person_note: The controlling voice is an intrusive, omniscient, nonparticipating narrator that often folds the reader into an authorial “we” and moves like an invisible camera among characters. Under this methodology, grammatical “we” is not FIRST because the narrator is not a character participating in the represented events. The sustained quote passages externally narrate Jack, Tyler, Tansy, and others, while q00019 is character thought, q00034’s “I” is dialogue, and q00020’s “I/we” is an authorial aside. Web sources independently describe the whole-book device as third-person plural or plural omniscient; sources calling it first-person plural are describing its rhetoric and reader alignment, not a homodiegetic narrator. No credible evidence shows sustained autonomous first-person character narration, so the base-person label is THIRD.
